prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of magic-angle flat bands and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Twisted bilayer graphene is the case in this shortlist where a specific quantitative prediction was followed by a decisive experimental discovery. Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted in 2011 that a continuum moire model gives flat bands at a magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's group found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle in 2018. The result has since been reproduced by many independent groups and extended to other moire platforms. It is also the candidate with the broadest support in the opening ballots: all seven members who ranked it placed it in the top five, three of them at rank two, and nobody argued against it. I ranked it third in my own opening ballot, behind the IceCube and reactor-neutrino candidates. After reading colleagues' arguments I think a prize with a theory-plus-experiment chain and this much consensus is the stronger configuration to carry forward, since my own first choice has little support.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is maturity and attribution. The discovery is only about seven years old, and the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so the prize would reward the existence of the phenomena and the platform, not a settled explanation. Attribution is also imperfect, since the 2018 experiments had co-first authors (Cao, Fatemi and others) who are outside the three-person limit, and Dean and collaborators contributed related moire work. A prize in 2026 might also be judged early compared with topological insulators, which have two decades of confirmation.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked topological insulators (B048) third, and judged the omission of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction the main attribution problem. He ranked twisted bilayer graphene (B016) second, calling the theory-plus-experiment split coherent but noting the missing Cao-type experimental credit.
responses.response: I agree that the BHZ omission is a serious weakness for B048. Molenkamp's HgTe experiment was a test of the BHZ prediction, not of Kane and Mele's graphene proposal, so a three-name B048 prize credits a theory and an experiment that do not directly connect. The B016 gap is real too, but smaller. Bistritzer and MacDonald's model is exactly what Jarillo-Herrero's group tested, so the chain is direct, and the co-first-author problem is one the committee already handles routinely. This is why I move B016 ahead of B048 even though B048 has more first-place votes.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked topological insulators first, as a clean pairing of theory and a decisive experiment that is mature and arguably overdue. He ranked the IceCube candidate (B047) only eighth.
responses.response: I accept that B048 is the more mature topological case and I do not dismiss it, which is why I list it as an alternative. My qualification is the one above: the maturity argument does not repair the BHZ gap in the credited names. On IceCube I accept his low ranking. I ranked it first, but only he and I ranked it at all, and I should not let a first-place vote from a field close to my own carry a prize that the committee as a whole does not support. I do not move to B047 in this round.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked dynamical mean-field theory first and twisted bilayer graphene second, calling the pairing a rare theory-plus-experiment case with large conceptual reach, though timing is somewhat early.
responses.response: We agree on the science and on the timing caveat. I give the early-timing concern more weight than he does, because the pairing mechanism is open. I would still not wait: the question for a Nobel prize is whether the discovery is established, and the correlated insulators and the superconducting domes have been reproduced widely. I do not share his first-place choice of DMFT, since the credit problems around Metzner and Jarrell are unresolved and the three-name set is imperfect.

responses.point: Kroll and Lindroth both ranked the optical lattice clock (B049) first, citing more than two decades of independent confirmation, a clean two-person credit and the coming redefinition of the second.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case, and I ranked it fourth in my opening ballot for the same reasons. The two-name credit is cleaner than for B016, and the maturity is greater. My reservation is that Katori and Ye share the field with other strontium and ytterbium groups and with the earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock work, and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. I would consider B049 a good prize and I name it as an alternative, but I do not think its two first-place votes outweigh the breadth of support for B016.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges seven years of confirmation sufficient, given the unsettled pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene.
How to handle the Cao co-first-author and Dean contributions within a three-person limit.
Whether B048 can be repaired by a different credited set that includes Bernevig, Hughes or Zhang, which the supplied names do not allow.
Whether the lattice-clock prize (B049) would be judged more mature and cleaner than B016 once credit to other clock groups is examined.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B016, B048 or B049. My documented collaborations are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, none of which involve the credited names. The IceCube candidate (B047) is close to my own field of astroparticle physics, though I have no documented IceCube connection. I note that as a field proximity, and not as a recusal ground.
